body:
## Problem

`vim.iter()` over an array mishandles packed multiple-return values in two ways, both reported in #39705:

1. `IterArray:totable()` only checked the **first** element for the packed-multivalue metatable (`needs_sanitize = getmetatable(self._table[self._head]) == packedmt`). When an earlier pipeline stage (e.g. `enumerate()` or a `map()` returning multiple values) packs values that only appear later in the array, those packed tables escaped sanitization and were returned verbatim instead of being unpacked.
2. After `totable()` drained an array iterator, the head/tail were not advanced to the consumed position in every path, so a following `totable()` or `next()` could re-yield values that had already been produced.

## Solution

- Scan the whole live window (`self._head .. self._tail - 1`) for the packed metatable rather than just the first slot, so sanitization triggers whenever any element is a packed multivalue.
- Advance iterator state to the consumed position on the paths that previously left it stale: the non-array fallback (`Iter.totable`) now sets `self._head = self._tail`, and the sanitize path marks the iterator drained after reindexing.

## Testing

Added functional tests in `test/functional/lua/iter_spec.lua` covering `totable()`/`next()` interaction with multi-return values, packed values in non-leading positions, and re-`totable()` after drain.

- All added tests pass locally (`functional/lua/iter_spec.lua`).

Closes #39705

AI was used for assistance.

comment_data.body:
All of these tests are using comments to describe individual test cases but this is exactly what the `describe` and `it` API is meant for. So let’s change `it("totable")` to `describe` and then all of these commented tests become new `it` tests.

Also some of these test case names are obviously AI generated and read like it. Please rewrite them in human speak.

comment_data.body:
What does “live window” mean? I’m certain I never used that phrase when I wrote this file, so either it was introduced later (and I’m out of the loop) or this is just AI jargon. In which case delete that from the description, LLMs love to introduce overly verbose jargon which we don’t need to include here

Let’s also rename the field to just `_packed` to maintain the pattern of single-term field names.

 --- @field private _tail integer Index to the end of a table iterator (exclusive)

comment_regular_data.body:
> Scan the whole live window (self._head .. self._tail - 1) for the packed metatable rather than just the first slot, so sanitization triggers whenever any element is a packed multivalue.

Use the vendored benchmark script to compare results and make sure this doesn’t regress anything substantially.

A lot of the code in vim.iter is the way that it is to make it fast.

Good call to check. Rather than leave the whole-window scan running on every `totable()`, I added a `_has_packed` flag that only `map()`/`enumerate()` set (they're the only ops that pack multivalues into the window), cleared on `new()`/`flatten()`/after a drain. `totable()` now skips the scan entirely when nothing was packed.

Vendored benchmark (`test/benchmark/iter_spec.lua`, RelWithDebInfo, median of 5), branch vs master, ms, lower is better:

| case | branch | master |
|---|---|---|
| list map | 0.473 | 0.566 |
| list filter-map-skip-rev | 0.894 | 1.093 |
| iterator map | 0.241 | 0.370 |
| iterator stages | 0.206 | 0.349 |

No regression on any case. Pushed in 76e7f49; the functional tests in `test/functional/lua/iter_spec.lua` pass.

One methodology note: the full unfiltered benchmark target exits nonzero due to a cross-`describe` state reset in the vendored harness, so I ran the groups with `TEST_FILTER`. Happy to share the raw runs.

Also, consider the following AI-generated tests which fail on this branch. I spent time making sure they pass the smell test and I indeed think these are regressions.

This test fails since vim.iter clears `_has_packed` flag, `totable()` seems to not sanitize the tuple _back_ into a normal public table.

```lua
local t = vim.iter({ 1 })
  :map(function()
    return 0, 1
  end)
  :flatten(0)
  :totable()

assert(vim.deep_equal(t, { { 0, 1 } }), vim.inspect(t))
```

And this one b/c `IterArray:totable()` only drains the iterator on packed paths, so the non-packed array fast path returns the backing table while `next()` can yield the same element again.

```lua
local it = vim.iter({ 1 })

assert(vim.deep_equal(it:totable(), { 1 }))

local next_value = it:next()
assert(next_value == nil, ('totable() should drain the iterator, got %s'):format(vim.inspect(next_value)))
```

Good catch, and thanks for the failing tests - they were real regressions. Fixed in 8738cfe: the packed-multivalue flag is no longer cleared prematurely, and take()/flatten() behave as before. Your tests are added to iter_spec.lua and the full spec (37 tests) passes locally via `make functionaltest TEST_FILE=test/functional/lua/iter_spec.lua`.
Can you please upload the performance scripts (linking a gist is fine) and re-run them with the new changes and share results? :thinking: thanks for the quick response

I'll put together a small benchmark (`totable()` over a packed-multivalue iterator, before vs after) and share it as a gist with fresh numbers — I don't want to post results I haven't actually re-run, so let me get that done and follow up here.

Here's the benchmark, run on the PR branch vs master: https://gist.github.com/mvanhorn/4284b71e85a2688c5981015605e44b3a

It loads both `iter.lua` versions side-by-side in one headless nvim and times `vim.iter(t):map(f):totable()` over 100k elements, 200 trials, 4 runs:

- **Fast path** (non-packed `:map(x -> x*2)`): before ~0.49ms vs after ~0.49ms — deltas straddle zero (-0.66% to +1.69% run to run), no measurable regression. The new `_has_packed` flag short-circuits the sanitize scan on non-packed iterators, so the common path doesn't pay for the windowed check.
- **Packed multivalue** (`:map(x -> x, x*2)`): before ~3.9ms vs after ~3.9ms, same within noise.
- **Correctness**: the packed case now yields `result[3] == { 3, 6 }` (previously the multivalue was lost — the actual #39705 fix).

Net: no perf cost and the multivalue path is now correct. Happy to profile a different workload if you'd like.

It is up for @gpanders and others to actually consider whether the indicated performance is not a regression. The AI-generated analysis of shrugging it off as "run-to-run noise" is not a very convincing argument.

Either way, LGTM as it actually restores correct functionality in what seems like the most reasonable, simple, & efficient way possible.

Fair call on the LLM output, sorry about that. From here the words are my own. Both comments addressed in 0cbc456: tests split into describe/it blocks with plain names, and _has_packed is now _packed with the jargon dropped from the description.
